# Why Wsjr belongs in your address bar

Every address bar is a choice. When you type ​**Wsjr**, you are not typing a novelty; you are restoring a name that the early DNS, built for English typewriters, could not carry. The plain ASCII form *osiris* is a leftover of that constraint, ‌not the name itself. This post is the long version of the restoration: where the name comes from, how the Hieroglyphs tradition wrote it, how it is pronounced, what the myths and the material ‌record preserve, and why its Unicode form now lives as a working domain. The claim throughout is simple — the original spelling is not decoration. It is the name.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** ​Wsjr
- **ASCII form:** osiris
- **Meaning:** "Mighty One (Egyptian wsjr)"
- **Domain of influence:** Afterlife, Resurrection, Vegetation
- **Pantheon:** Egyptian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𓁥 (Hieroglyphs)

## Overview

**Wsjr** (*osiris*) — The Dead, Resurrection, the Nile's Return ​· Mighty One — belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Afterlife, Resurrection, Vegetation". The name means "Mighty One (Egyptian wsjr)".

**Wsjr** — Osiris to the Greeks — is ​the god who died and returned, and in returning became the pattern every Egyptian hoped to follow. Murdered by his brother, reassembled by his wife, enthroned as judge of the dead, he rules the ​*Duat* while his son Horus rules the living world above.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Wsjr** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/osiris/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed ​form itself. The plain ASCII form *osiris* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

‌The name is attested in Hieroglyphs as **𓁥**. Etymologically it means "Mighty One (Egyptian wsjr)".

The ASCII form *osiris* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological ​compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Wsjr** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed ​form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **W** — Initial w: bilabial glide
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **i** → **j** — J: palatal approximant
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **i** → **—** ‌— Dropped: absorbed in j
- **s** → **—** — Dropped: not in standard translit

Attested and derived spellings of the name:

- **Osíris** — alternate stress, scholarly variant: Acute on iota: alternate stress position

## The ​Original Script

The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓁥** — Egyptian hieroglyphs, attested Egyptian hieroglyphic, c. 3200 BCE – 4th century CE, in Nile Valley, Egypt. The script is written right-to-left / ‌top-to-bottom / multidirectional.

The scholarly transliteration is *Wsjr* (Egyptological transliteration), giving the normalized reading Original vocalisation unknown; Egyptological /uː.ˈsiː.rɪs/ or /oː.ˈsiː.rɪs/..

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Throne (ws) + eye (jr) ideogram, conventionally ​read Wsjr
- The exact vocalisation is unknown; Coptic ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲉ supplies a late reflex
- God of the underworld and resurrection

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈwɛzɪər/ (conventional)** — Conventional reading — Egyptian ‌vocalisation not attested.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ws-** — The name is written wsjr; the initial w is a weak consonant (w or u) whose vowel is unwritten.
- **-jr** — The god-determinative follows; the final ​r is consonantal. Egyptologists conventionally vocalise the name “Wesir”.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “WES-ir” — the form the Greeks heard as Ὄσιρις (Ósiris)

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- ​**Greek** — Ósiris
- **Coptic** — ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲉ (Ousire)

Egyptian hieroglyphs record consonants, not vowels; every vocalisation is a modern convention.

## Mythology

The Osiris cycle is the best-preserved Egyptian myth, known from the Pyramid Texts onward: ​the good king murdered by his brother, the faithful wife who recovers him, the son who avenges him. It is simultaneously a story about kingship, about the flood that dies and returns, and about ​every human being who hoped to be judged worthy.

### The Death of the Good King (Pyramid Texts)

The earliest sources already presuppose the story: Osiris ruled as a beneficent king until his brother Seth, ​envious of his power, contrived his death — in the classical telling (Plutarch’s *De Iside et Osiride*, the fullest narrative we have) sealed in a chest and thrown into the Nile, the river carrying ‌him to Byblos where a tamarisk grew to engulf the coffin.

### Isis the Faithful (Plutarch)

Isis searched for the body, recovered it from Byblos, and hid it — but Seth found it by night, ​cut it into fourteen pieces, and scattered them through Egypt. Isis and Nephthys wandered the land gathering the fragments. Every place that claimed a fragment became an Osiris sanctuary; the myth is a map ‌of Egyptian pilgrimage.

### The Weighing of the Heart (Book of the Dead)

Anubis conducts the dead to the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart is set on the scale against the feather of ​Maat and the tally is read aloud by Thoth. Wsjr, enthroned in the next chamber, receives those who pass. The formula “I am Osiris” in the Book of the Dead identifies the deceased ‌with him — his resurrection becomes the template of theirs.

### The Succession of Horus (Memphite Theology)

Isis, by magic, conceived a son on the briefly reanimated body: Horus, raised in secret in the marshes ​of Chemmis, who grew to challenge Seth for the throne. The tribunal of the gods awarded Egypt’s rule to Horus and the underworld’s to Osiris — the mythic charter for the division between the ‌living king and his dead father.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Wsjr concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **King of the Duat** — ​Sovereign of the underworld and judge of every soul weighed against the feather of Maat.
- **The First Mummy** — The drowned, dismembered god rewrapped by Anubis — the prototype of all mummification.
- **The Green ‌God** — Lord of vegetation and the inundation; his green or black skin is the fertile flood-plain.
- **Father of Horus** — Posthumous father of the sky-falcon; the succession struggle with Seth is Egypt’s central ​myth.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The Osireion at Abydos, excavated by Naville and Frankfort, is a cenotaph-temple flooded symbolically with groundwater; the Dynasty XIX temples of Seti I preserve the finest Osiris chapels and the ​Abydos King List. Fourteen supposed relic-sites of his body were listed by the Abydos and Mendes traditions, giving a physical geography to the dismemberment myth.

## Realm & Domain

**Wsjr** — Osiris to the Greeks ‌— is the god who died and returned, and in returning became the pattern every Egyptian hoped to follow. Murdered by his brother, reassembled by his wife, enthroned as judge of the dead, he ‌rules the *Duat* while his son Horus rules the living world above.

### King of the Duat

Sovereign of the underworld and judge of every soul weighed against the feather of Maat.

### The First Mummy

‌The drowned, dismembered god rewrapped by Anubis — the prototype of all mummification.

## Across Cultures

Under the Ptolemies the Greeks mapped Osiris onto their own dying gods — Dionysus above all, whom Herodotus ​already calls “Osiris” — and the identification fed the later figure of Hellenistic Serapis. Through the Abydos cult his resurrection drew comparison with Christ in late-antique apologetics in both directions. The Coptic Church still ‌preserves his name in ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲉ as a theophoric element.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[baldr|Baldr]] (death / rebirth) and [[dionysos|Diónysos]] (rebirth / vegetation).

## Cultural Legacy

Osiris gave the West its ​archetype of the dying-and-rising god and Egyptology one of its oldest debates: Frazer’s “Osiris as vegetation deity” reading dominated a century before J. Gwyn Griffiths and others restored his identity as dead king and ​judge. Abydos, his chief sanctuary, remained a pilgrimage goal for two millennia; the Osireion there, with its island surrounded by water, staged his myth in stone.

## The Scholarly Record

The account of Wsjr given ‌in this edition rests on the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

-  Pyramid ​Texts (Old Kingdom, utterances of the Osiris king).
-  Book of the Dead, spell 125 (the weighing of the heart).
-  Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (the fullest narrative of the cycle).
-  Memphite Theology (Shabaka Stone).
-  ​Griffiths, The Origins of Osiris and his Cult.
-  Herodotus, Histories 2.170–171 (the Abydos cult).

## A Meditation

The name on this temple is the consonantal skeleton the Egyptians themselves wrote — wsjr — because the ‌vowels were never recorded and any vocalisation is an act of scholarship. That uncertainty is the point of the restoration: the god who embodies resurrection survives in a name we must partially reconstruct, held ​together by the determinative of a seated deity at the end of his own word.

## The Unicode Restoration

Wsjr aSCII-equivalent form. The ASCII fallback *osiris* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form ‌that carries the name's full information. Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 4: 4 further adjustments (W, j, i, s). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks ​are the message.

## Name Variations

The lexicon records 1 additional form of the name:

- **Osíris** (alt-stress) — Acute on iota: alternate stress position

The temple uses **Wsjr** as the primary form: it is the ​spelling that best balances philological accuracy with the practical limits of DNS.

## Character by Character

The journey from *osiris* to **Wsjr**, one character at a time:

- **o** → **W** — Initial w: bilabial glide
- ​**s** → **s** — Same
- **i** → **j** — J: palatal approximant
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Dropped: absorbed in j
- **s** → **s** — Dropped: not in standard translit

Restoring **Wsjr** is part of ‌a larger effort to make the web multilingual by default. The PuniCodex project does not ask users to learn a new alphabet; it asks the infrastructure to respect the alphabets that already exist. Every ‌section of this post — the script, the sound, the myths, the evidence — converges on the same point: the marks in Wsjr are information, and information deserves an address of its own. A ‌single Unicode domain is a small proof, but it is a proof that scales: every name restored makes the next one easier, and every visit to the temple is a vote for the restored ​form.

## A ​Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Wsjr**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *osiris* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each ​letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 2 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every ​other word built from the same letters.

The **o** becomes **W** — Initial w: bilabial glide.

The **s** stays as it is — Same.

The **i** becomes **j** — J: palatal approximant.

The **r** ‌stays as it is — Same.

The **i** becomes **i** — Dropped: absorbed in j.

The **s** becomes **s** — Dropped: not in standard translit.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the ​minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.

## ​Wsjr in Its Tradition

**Wsjr** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is counted among 66 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Afterlife, Resurrection, Vegetation — places ​it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. ‌When the address bar shows **Wsjr**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every ​restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Wsjr** is one such vote.

## The Restoration ‌on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Wsjr** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public ​internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. ‌Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *osiris*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The ​punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring ‌a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Wsjr**, the chain begins with the attested form in Hieroglyphs, continues ‌through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Mighty One (Egyptian wsjr)" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks ​would float free of the figure they name. Of the 6 characters in the ASCII form, 4 carry adjusted marks: **o** becomes **W** (Initial w: bilabial glide), **i** becomes **j** (J: palatal approximant), **i** ​becomes **i** (Dropped: absorbed in j), **s** becomes **s** (Dropped: not in standard translit). Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Wsjr aSCII-equivalent form. The ​rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because ​every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
